complexity_matrix.operation: Index access arr[i] on contiguous storage
complexity_matrix.notes: Address is computed as base + i * sizeof(element): one multiply, one add. No search, no loop.
O(1) amortised by charging each doubling's O(C) copy across the C appends that filled it. Worst case for a single append is the resize itself.
Full copy of every existing element, plus allocation of a buffer twice the old capacity. Amortised over the growth sequence this is O(1) per append.

complexity_matrix.operation: Insert or delete at an arbitrary interior index k
complexity_matrix.notes: Trailing elements must shift to keep the layout gap-free. Best case O(1) is append-like insertion at the final index.
Expected cost is 1 + alpha, where alpha is the load factor. Worst case is a full collision into one bucket.
Same expected 1 + alpha cost; both operations may additionally trigger a rehash of every entry.

complexity_matrix.operation: Resize the bucket array and rehash all entries
complexity_matrix.notes: Every stored key is rehashed into a bucket twice the old count. Amortised across the growth sequence this is O(1) per insert.

complexity_matrix.operation: Iterate all keys in sorted order
complexity_matrix.notes: A hash table destroys key order, so producing sorted output requires an external sort over the whole key set.

complexity_matrix.operation: Range query over keys in [a, b]
complexity_matrix.notes: Keys are scattered across buckets arbitrarily, so there is no contiguity to exploit. This is the cost of choosing hashing.

complexity_matrix.operation: Total space for N stored entries
complexity_matrix.notes: Bucket array is Theta(N / alpha) words plus a key, value and chaining pointer per entry. Strictly more than an array of N primitives.

correctness_argument.claim: Lookup is correct because equal keys must hash equal, which places a present key in the searched bucket, and every entry is reachable from its own bucket; a scan that finds nothing therefore proves absence.

cost_derivations.claim: Charging each capacity-doubling resize across the appends since the previous one makes append O(1) amortised, while a single append remains O(N) worst case; hash lookup costs 1 + alpha expected, where alpha is the entry-to-bucket ratio.

limits.claim: No deterministic worst-case O(1) hash lookup is known in general. The Omega(N log N) comparison-sorting barrier does not apply, because hashing computes positions arithmetically rather than by comparing keys.
